title: A 70-Year Dig Unlocks an Ancient City's Secrets!
summary: Have you ever dug a hole in your backyard hoping to find treasure? Now imagine doing that for 70 years straight! That's what archaeologists have been doing at Sardis, an ancient city in Turkey. And their hard work just paid off big time: Sardis is now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Sardis was once the capital of Lydia, a kingdom famous for inventing the very first coins. Its king, Croesus, was so rich that we still say "rich as Croesus" today! Later, Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, and Ottomans all ruled the city. Because it was never buried under a modern city, layers of history are just waiting to be uncovered. Since 1958, a team from Harvard and Cornell has returned every year. They've found amazing things: a huge bath-gymnasium, the biggest ancient synagogue ever discovered, a gold workshop, and even a shopping district! Recently, they uncovered a sanctuary plaza that took 15 years to dig out. But the early days of digging weren't so careful. In the 1900s, explorers took artifacts away, including a giant column now in a New York museum. Today, archaeologists work with local communities to preserve and share what they find. "This project has always wanted to make their work understandable to tourists and locals," says Professor Benjamin Anderson. Now, with UNESCO status, Sardis will be protected and shared with the whole world. It's a place where you can walk through 4,000 years of history — all because some people kept digging.
why_it_matters: Every shovel of dirt at Sardis teaches us that history is not just in books—it’s buried beneath our feet, and caring for it can connect you to people who lived thousands of years ago.

background_read: UNESCO (the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) gives ‘World Heritage’ status to places that tell an important part of human history, like the Pyramids or the Great Wall.

Long ago, Sardis was the capital of Lydia, where people created the first coins around 600 BC. Because different empires built their cities on the same spot, the layers of dirt hold clues about thousands of years of life.
Article_Structure: WHO: Archaeologists from Harvard and Cornell, and Professor Benjamin Anderson
WHAT: After 70 years of digging, Sardis became a UNESCO World Heritage site, with huge finds like a synagogue, shops, and a gold workshop
WHERE: The ancient city of Sardis in Turkey
WHY: To protect the city’s 4,000-year history and share it with the world

perspectives.description: Finding a whole ancient city untouched under the ground is a dream. Now as a protected UNESCO site, it will be safe for future generations to study and enjoy.
In the old days, outsiders took away beautiful artifacts. Some might feel that even today, the local community should have a bigger say in how their history is shown.
I can’t wait to visit Sardis one day and walk on streets where kings and merchants lived 2,500 years ago. It makes history feel real, not just a story.
